evidence.questionPrompt: 1. {{1}}: Homo sapiens originated in Africa and eventually spread to every continent including Antarctica.
evidence.sourceTitle: Reading — Passage 1: The Patterns of Human Migration
evidence.sourceExcerpt: Migration—the movement of people from one place to another—is among the most powerful forces shaping human societies. It is also one of the most ancient: Homo sapiens emerged in Africa approximately three hundred thousand years ago and, over tens of thousands of years, dispersed across every continent except Antarctica. The story of modern migration is continuous with this prehistoric movement, driven by the same fundamental forces: the search for safety, sustenance, and opportunity. Modern statistics, however, require careful interpretation. A migrant stock counts people living outside their country of birth at a particular time, whereas a migration flow records journeys during a period. Nor are categories always mutually exclusive: someone may move for work after first leaving home because of conflict or drought.

evidence.questionPrompt: 2. {{2}}: In 2022, remittances sent by migrants exceeded the total value of official development aid.
evidence.sourceTitle: Reading — Passage 1: The Patterns of Human Migration
evidence.sourceExcerpt: Contemporary migration takes many forms. Labour migration refers to the movement of workers, often from lower-income to higher-income countries, in search of better employment opportunities. The World Migration Report 2024 cites an estimate of approximately 281 million international migrants worldwide in 2020, representing about 3.6 percent of the global population. It also reports that international remittances—money sent home by migrants—totalled $831 billion in 2022. Of that sum, $647 billion went to low- and middle-income countries, far exceeding official development aid and constituting a vital economic lifeline for many households and national economies.

evidence.questionPrompt: 3. {{3}}: By the end of 2023, more than half of all forcibly displaced people had crossed an international border.
evidence.sourceTitle: Reading — Passage 1: The Patterns of Human Migration
evidence.sourceExcerpt: Forced migration, by contrast, involves movement driven by persecution, conflict, violence, or events that seriously disturb public order rather than primarily by economic calculation. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees reported that by the end of 2023, 117.3 million people were forcibly displaced—the highest figure then recorded. The total included 68.3 million internally displaced people, who had not crossed a national border, and 43.4 million refugees and other people needing international protection. A further 6.9 million were asylum-seekers awaiting decisions on their claims. These figures cannot simply be divided into refugees and internally displaced people, because the overall population contains several legal and statistical categories. Major refugee populations included people from Syria, Afghanistan, and Ukraine, while Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine produced one of the fastest displacement events in modern history.

evidence.questionPrompt: 4. {{4}}: People displaced by climate change are fully protected under the 1951 Refugee Convention.
evidence.sourceTitle: Reading — Passage 1: The Patterns of Human Migration
evidence.sourceExcerpt: Environmental migration—movement associated with climate change, sea-level rise, and extreme weather events—is an increasingly significant phenomenon that existing international legal frameworks were not designed to address directly. People displaced solely by environmental factors do not qualify as refugees under the 1951 Refugee Convention, whose definition rests on a well-founded fear of persecution. Some people move temporarily after a storm; others relocate within their own country after repeated crop failures; and a smaller group crosses a border when living conditions become untenable. This variety makes the phenomenon difficult to measure and has left many environmental migrants without the protections accorded to Convention refugees.

evidence.questionPrompt: 5. {{5}}: Immigrants and their children have founded a large proportion of major US companies.
evidence.sourceTitle: Reading — Passage 1: The Patterns of Human Migration
evidence.sourceExcerpt: The social and economic effects of migration on receiving countries are complex and contested. Research generally shows that, in aggregate, migration can increase the economic output of receiving countries: migrants fill labour shortages, bring skills and entrepreneurship, and contribute to fiscal revenues through taxation. One analysis of the 2017 Fortune 500 found that 18.4 percent of those companies had been founded by immigrants and another 24.8 percent by their children. Separate research has also found that immigrant-founded firms account for a disproportionately high share of patents and innovation. However, aggregate benefits can mask distributional effects: employers and consumers may gain while some workers in direct competition with new arrivals face wage pressure. Outcomes depend on migrants' skills, local labour demand, and how quickly housing and public services adjust.

Qubits are extraordinarily sensitive to their environment: any interaction with external factors—heat, electromagnetic radiation, even vibration—causes decoherence, a process in which the quantum state collapses prematurely. evidence.questionPrompt: How was the placebo effect primarily viewed during most of the twentieth century?
evidence.sourceExcerpt: In clinical medicine, a placebo is an inert treatment—a sugar pill, a saline injection, or a sham procedure—that contains no active pharmacological ingredient. The placebo effect refers to measurable improvement associated with receiving such a treatment and with the context surrounding it. Researchers must distinguish changes in a patient's reported symptoms from changes in the underlying disease: pain or nausea may ease even when a tumour, infection, or damaged tissue is unaffected. They must also separate a true response from natural recovery, fluctuating symptoms, and the statistical tendency for unusually severe symptoms to move back towards their average level. For most of the twentieth century, the placebo effect was regarded primarily as a nuisance variable in clinical trials—something to be subtracted from the results to identify the effect of an active drug. More recent research has made it a clinically significant phenomenon in its own right.

evidence.questionPrompt: What did brain imaging studies show about placebo analgesia?
evidence.sourceExcerpt: The magnitude of the placebo effect varies considerably depending on the condition, the context, and the manner in which the treatment is administered. In trials of antidepressants, placebo response rates are frequently between thirty and forty-five percent—high enough that some researchers have questioned whether the active benefit of many widely prescribed medications, over and above placebo, is clinically meaningful for mild to moderate depression. For pain conditions, placebo analgesia is well documented: patients receiving an inert injection have shown measurable reductions in subjective pain scores, and brain imaging studies have demonstrated that placebos activate the same endogenous opioid pathways as actual analgesic drugs. The brain, it appears, can produce its own pain-relieving chemicals in response to the expectation of relief.

evidence.questionPrompt: What is the key finding of "open-label placebo" research?
evidence.sourceExcerpt: The expectation of benefit is widely considered the core mechanism of the placebo effect, but it is not the only one. Classical conditioning also plays a role: if a patient has previously responded well to a treatment, the ritual of receiving any similar treatment—the clinical environment, the manner of the prescriber, the act of swallowing a pill—can trigger a conditioned therapeutic response. Research by Ted Kaptchuk at Harvard Medical School has produced the counterintuitive finding that placebos can be effective even when patients are told explicitly that they are receiving an inert treatment, a phenomenon known as "open-label placebo" or OLP. Participants in several OLP trials reported significant improvements in conditions including irritable bowel syndrome and chronic lower back pain, apparently because the ritual of receiving treatment retained some therapeutic power independent of belief.

evidence.questionPrompt: What does the nocebo effect demonstrate, according to the passage?
evidence.sourceExcerpt: Research on the nocebo effect—the counterpart to the placebo effect, in which negative expectations produce adverse outcomes—adds further complexity. Patients who are warned about the side effects of a drug are more likely to experience them, even when given a placebo instead of the drug. In one notable study, patients randomised to a placebo arm in a cardiac trial who believed they might be receiving a beta-blocker were significantly more likely to report fatigue—the key side effect of beta-blockers—than placebo patients who did not hold this belief. The nocebo effect has practical implications for informed consent: detailed disclosure of side effects may not only inform patients but, paradoxically, cause the very symptoms it describes. Clinicians therefore face a communication problem. They must describe material risks honestly while presenting probabilities in a balanced way that does not magnify fear or imply that adverse effects are inevitable.

evidence.questionPrompt: 36. {{36}}: Warning patients about side effects can sometimes cause them to experience those symptoms.
evidence.sourceExcerpt: Research on the nocebo effect—the counterpart to the placebo effect, in which negative expectations produce adverse outcomes—adds further complexity. Patients who are warned about the side effects of a drug are more likely to experience them, even when given a placebo instead of the drug. In one notable study, patients randomised to a placebo arm in a cardiac trial who believed they might be receiving a beta-blocker were significantly more likely to report fatigue—the key side effect of beta-blockers—than placebo patients who did not hold this belief. The nocebo effect has practical implications for informed consent: detailed disclosure of side effects may not only inform patients but, paradoxically, cause the very symptoms it describes. Clinicians therefore face a communication problem. They must describe material risks honestly while presenting probabilities in a balanced way that does not magnify fear or imply that adverse effects are inevitable.
